intro: やら and だの both list a few examples out of a bigger, messier set, and both are normally repeated after every item: AやらBやら, AだのBだの. What they add is feeling. やら says the speaker is swamped by a jumble of things or emotions; だの says the speaker is fed up with a string of things someone keeps saying or wanting.

skills.rule: AやらBやら lists a couple of examples from a chaotic pile of things, events or feelings that overwhelm the speaker.
skills.explain:
やら picks two or three items out of a larger heap and makes it sound like a lot going on at once: 会議やら出張やらで忙しい (busy with meetings, business trips and whatnot). It is very often followed by で, giving the cause of a state: what with A and B.

It attaches to nouns, to plain-form verbs and to i-adjectives, so it can list actions and feelings, not only things: 泣くやら騒ぐやら (crying, making a racket), 嬉しいやら恥ずかしいやら (happy and embarrassed at once). That last use, mixed emotions the speaker cannot sort out, is a set phrase pattern.

や and とか also give examples, but neutrally; や joins nouns only and is not repeated after the last item. やら carries confusion or bewilderment, so it fits descriptions of a situation, not requests or instructions. Unlike だの it is not about complaining at someone; the speaker is simply swamped.
patterns: [plain verb] やら [plain verb] やら で [state]

examples.jp: 部屋[へや]には本[ほん]{やら}服[ふく]{やら}が散[ち]らかっていた。
examples.en: Books, clothes and whatnot were scattered round the room.

examples.jp: 今週[こんしゅう]は会議[かいぎ]{やら}出張[しゅっちょう]{やら}で忙[いそが]しい。
examples.en: This week I'm busy with meetings, business trips and so on.

examples.jp: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]しの日[ひ]は、掃除[そうじ]{やら}荷造[にづく]り{やら}で一日[いちにち]が終[お]わった。
examples.en: On moving day the whole day went on cleaning, packing and the like.

examples.jp: 子供[こども]たちが泣[な]く{やら}騒[さわ]ぐ{やら}で大変[たいへん]だった。
examples.en: What with the children crying and making a racket, it was chaos.

examples.jp: 褒[ほ]められて、嬉[うれ]しい{やら}恥[は]ずかしい{やら}で顔[かお]が赤[あか]くなった。
examples.en: When I was praised I went red, half pleased and half embarrassed.

contrast.note: 本や服 lists examples neutrally, nouns only, with nothing after the last item. 本やら服やら adds a sense of mess and is repeated.
とか is the casual neutral example marker and fits requests: 果物とか買ってきて. やら describes an overwhelming situation.
だの lists what someone keeps saying or demanding, with irritation. やら is the speaker's own jumble of things or feelings.

mistakes.bad: りんご{やら}バナナ{やら}を買[か]ってきてください。
mistakes.good: りんご{とか}バナナ{とか}を買[か]ってきてください。
mistakes.note: やら describes a chaotic situation; for neutral examples in a request use とか or や.

mistakes.bad: 嬉[うれ]しい{だの}恥[は]ずかしい{だの}で顔[かお]が赤[あか]くなった。
mistakes.good: 嬉[うれ]しい{やら}恥[は]ずかしい{やら}で顔[かお]が赤[あか]くなった。
mistakes.note: Your own mixed feelings take やら; だの would mean someone is complaining.

skills.tip: Could you add all at once, and it's too much? Then it is やら.

skills.rule: AだのBだの lists the things someone keeps saying, demanding or fussing about, and shows that the speaker is annoyed by it.
skills.explain:
だの strings together examples of what another person says or wants, and the speaker's tone is critical: 暑いだの疲れただのと文句ばかり言う (it's hot, I'm tired, nothing but complaints). It is very often followed by と plus a verb of saying or by うるさい: だのと言う, だのとうるさい.

It attaches to nouns, plain-form verbs and adjectives, and even to opposites: 行くだの行かないだの (going, not going, back and forth). The items are usually quoted words or wants; it can also list chores the speaker resents: 掃除だの洗濯だので忙しい.

The boundary with やら is whose problem it is. やら is the speaker caught in a jumble of tasks or feelings; だの is the speaker judging someone else's talk, or grumbling. とか can list the same quoted complaints, but neutrally; switch to だの only when you want the irritation to show. Because it is critical, だの is wrong in a neutral or positive list.
patterns: [quote] だの [quote] だの と [say / fuss]
[noun] だの [noun] だの と [want / demand]

examples.jp: 弟[おとうと]は暑[あつ]い{だの}疲[つか]れた{だの}と文句[もんく]ばかり言[い]う。
examples.en: My brother does nothing but complain: it's hot, he's tired, and so on.

examples.jp: 娘[むすめ]はゲーム{だの}服[ふく]{だの}と、欲[ほ]しがってばかりいる。
examples.en: My daughter is always wanting something: games, clothes, you name it.

examples.jp: 行[い]く{だの}行[い]かない{だの}と、彼[かれ]はなかなか決[き]めない。
examples.en: He's going, he's not going; he just can't make up his mind.

examples.jp: 部長[ぶちょう]は字[じ]が小[ちい]さい{だの}色[いろ]が暗[くら]い{だの}とうるさい。
examples.en: The manager keeps nagging: the writing is too small, the colours are too dark.

examples.jp: 高[たか]い{だの}遠[とお]い{だの}言[い]わないで、一度[いちど]行[い]ってみなさい。
examples.en: Stop saying it's too expensive or too far, and just go once.

contrast.note: やら is the speaker swamped by things or feelings. だの is the speaker irritated, usually by what someone else keeps saying.
暑いとか疲れたとか言う reports the same words neutrally. だの adds criticism of the person saying them.
や joins nouns in a neutral list and cannot follow verbs or quoted words. だの can follow anything someone says.

mistakes.bad: 旅行[りょこう]で寺[てら]{だの}神社[じんじゃ]{だの}を見[み]て、楽[たの]しかった。
mistakes.good: 旅行[りょこう]で寺[てら]{や}神社[じんじゃ]を見[み]て、楽[たの]しかった。
mistakes.note: だの is critical, so it clashes with a happy, neutral list. Use や or とか.

skills.tip: Can you hear an eye-roll and and on and on he goes? Then it is だの.
